intro.heading: The session went well. Half the team was off.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: After a resident's second fall in a month, the manager of a residential home holds a thirty minute session in the lounge on what to do in the first ten minutes. The senior who runs it is clear and calm. The carers on shift that Wednesday listen and ask good questions. But the home runs 12 hour days on a rota, and the carers who work the other days were at home. The manager means to brief them at handover. Then a busy week arrives, and the second session never quite happens. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A senior carer runs a falls session in the lounge.
The carers on shift ask good questions and leave knowing the steps.
The manager notes the session and promises the others a catch up.
The other team is on shift. The catch up is squeezed out by a hospital appointment.
A new agency carer starts, and nobody mentions the falls session.
A carer who thinks you can help a fallen resident up to check they are fine.
A session note for one team. No view of what the rest of the home knows.
“A resident falls at the weekend. What do you do?” The carer hesitates.

trail_close: The session was never the problem. The gap is between one team and the whole home. Here is how CareStream closes it using your own policies, without replacing the session.

cards.title: New starters and agency cover miss it

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Half my team missed the session. Do I have to run it twice?
items.a: You can keep running it as you do now. What you add is a short module on the same topic that every carer completes in the Staff Hub, whichever days they work. The session teaches. The module shows what each person took in, including the ones who were never in the room.

items.q: Where does the content come from?
items.a: From your own policies. You pick a topic module, and CareStream builds the lesson and questions from what your home has written, with general good practice as the fallback where a policy is silent. You can edit it and preview it before anyone is given it.

items.q: What happens when a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab in the hub, and they get an email, at most once a day and in English. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Do carers need to be on shift to do it?
items.a: No. It sits in the hub on their own phone, so they can open it when they have a few quiet minutes. You can set a due date when you allocate it. You decide how it fits their hours.

items.q: A lot of my carers speak English as a second language. Does that matter?
items.a: It matters. A carer may know exactly what to do and still miss one word in a question. On the paid plans they can open the lesson in their own language, so a wrong answer points to a gap in knowledge and not in vocabulary.

items.q: What do I see across the home?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view in Analytics shows open gaps, how many staff are affected, gaps closed in the last 30 days, and the most missed questions and weakest topics. A digest email arrives each Monday. Nothing messages you every time someone gets an answer wrong.

items.q: Does this replace watching someone do the task?
items.a: No. A competent person still needs to observe hands on skills, such as helping a resident up safely. CareStream checks understanding and keeps the record. It does not replace the observation, and it is not a pass or a rating.

faqs.heading: Residential care home training and CareStream, answered

items.q: How do I follow up residential care home training after a session?
items.a: Within a few days, allocate a short module on the same topic to everyone who needs it. Carers complete it on their phone, and a wrong answer becomes a short lesson and a fresh question. You then see the pattern in the Knowledge gaps view.

items.q: Can CareStream build training from our residential care home policies?
items.a: Yes. You pick a topic module and the lesson and questions draw on your own policies where they cover it. Where your policies do not, it falls back on general good practice, which is a sign a policy may need work. See policy gaps.

items.q: What should residential care home policies say about falls?
items.a: That is for your home to decide, based on your residents and your own risk assessments. Training only helps if it matches what your policy says, so the module is built from your wording rather than a generic script.

items.q: Does this cover induction and the Care Certificate?
items.a: It sits alongside them. New starters can be given short modules on topics from your policies. For the Care Certificate itself, see the Care Certificate course.

items.q: Does online follow up replace practical training?
items.a: No. Skills such as moving and handling need a competent person to show and observe the technique. The follow up checks that people understood and remembered.

items.q: What if a carer keeps getting the same question wrong?
items.a: They can keep retrying. If the same point keeps appearing in the Knowledge gaps view, treat it as information: it may need a conversation or clearer policy wording.

items.q: What does care home compliance mean for staff training?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal they need to carry out their duties. It does not list courses, so each provider decides what its staff need and must be able to show it.

items.q: What does CQC look for in residential care compliance?
items.a: The CQC guidance on Regulation 18 says training needs should be assessed at the start of employment and reviewed periodically, and that staff should be monitored with action taken when training is not completed. See also our guide to CQC evidence.

No product can. CareStream gives you a record of what was asked, what was missed and what was learned. That is evidence you can use, and it sits alongside observation, supervision and your audits. It is not a pass, a rating or a regulator record.

guide.heading: A practical way to run training across a rota
guide.lede: Residential care home training has to work for people who are never in the same room at once. The aim is simple: everyone gets the same message, and you find out who did not take it in.

sections.h3: Make the session the start, not the end
paragraphs: A session is strongest when it has a clear single topic and a named senior who can answer questions. Treat it as the first of two steps. The second is a short check, within a few days, for everyone who needs to know, including the people who were not there.
Keep a note of who was in the room. That becomes your allocation list. Our guide to running in house training and short learning on a 12 hour shift go further.

sections.h3: A weekly rhythm that fits a busy home
checklist: Same day: note who attended and who was off, so you know who needs the follow up.
Within a few days: allocate a short module on the topic to everyone on that list.
When an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each Monday: read the digest and look at the most missed questions and weakest topics.

sections.h3: Keep your policies and your training saying the same thing
paragraphs: Training that contradicts the policy on the shelf is worse than none. If the same question keeps being missed, check the wording of the policy first. It is often a sign the policy is long, vague or out of date. Our four question framework helps you decide who needs retraining when a policy changes, which also supports your wider care home compliance.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the lessons and the results together with your session notes, so you can show who understood, not only who attended.
